summary: The first III block uses active mašəġ- with possessed body parts, explicit ruḥo, an implicit self, and ordinary objects. Self-directed washing does not itself select Detransitive morphology. Objects may be zero-marked, l-marked (114/17; 113/157), or suffixed; b- marks instruments/liquids and m- a removed contaminant (JTM 2.13/2; 96/260).

The washing Detransitive contrasts an agentless procedure (rice, JTM 2.9/1) with a result predicate caused by rain (JTM 1.1/51) and an attributive washed-wheat form (JL 17.5/3). The already cited 112/155 is not a new example.

təšiġo/tešiġo/tušiġo are action nominals with d-marked patients or a suffix, in task, purpose and nominal-predicate frames. Use Infinitiv provisionally; the t-prefix alone does not establish a Detransitive reading.

Infectum-wa covers habitual procedures and interrupted background washing; completion in a procedural sequence can instead be expressed by Preterit or by context around Infectum. German past tense is not a box diagnostic.

The second III block mašək- codes an experiencer with the Preterit agent ending, a b-marked stimulus (78/10; 71/48; MAC NE Habirman Xatun/15), or content clauses (LuF 3/25; MAC NE Ditin Hazar/37). Do not pool its cells with washing.
Lookups: search tickle located only the mixed šyġ material; entry šyk returned no entry. No independent lexical destination was invented.

The 42 abbreviated synthesis records were checked against their full bracketed verses in inputs/texts (JTM, PrS, Ritter, MAC and Talay). All are ordinary washing in the recorded boxes; no missing-verse limitation remains.
All Jan English quoted here is project machine translation [MT]. Semantic assignments rest on the Turoyo washing and perception contexts.

The source entry contains two III blocks. Every delta stem and occurrence identifies stem_id: šyġ.III is washing mašəġle/mašəġ; šyġ.III~2 is noticing mašəkle/mašək. Round-1 separation and tickling-reassignment proposals remain in force and are not proposed again.

Ordinary washing Infectum, Infectum-wa, Imperativ and Infinitiv were filled in round 1. The sole washing addition is justified by the unusual suffix and overt washer/patient contrast, not the reader’s outdated thin-cell counts.
Self-washing can be expressed without ruḥo (Jan 2.4/801; 2.31/4976). It remains in the ordinary III boxes; a reflexive interpretation alone does not establish Detransitive morphology.
The human-patient suffixes -lən, -nne and -walle occur in the funeral sequence (Jan 1.15/575–577). Do not silently classify -lən as a beneficiary when the context asks about washing those people.
Repeated mašəġiwole during meat preparation (Jan 1.26/1270) can emphasize repeated/thorough washing. Repeated forms are separate occurrence records, not independent additions.

The noticing Preterit with bənne (Jan 1.45/1973) supports the same perception government as round 1. The Jan 3.10/108 Infectum-wa is new only within this noticing block; its positive/negative b mən pattern needs native interpretation.

summary: Washing applies to foods, wool, rooms, body parts, corpses and a filly; tears can supply the washing liquid. These participant and medium changes do not require separate senses.
Corpse washing and washing a deceased priest’s hands and feet remain literal washing, not a new ritual sense. They support the round-1 human-patient evidence.
təšiġo with clothes or dishes supports round 1’s action-nominal Infinitiv classification, including d lo təšiġo; it is not a new form box this round.
